Your guess: Which region has the highest typical daily sales? Which region is the least predictable from day to day? Do any regions have unusual days?

Step 1: A bar chart of averages

TipReveal the bar chart
Show the Python code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
            hue="region", palette=palette, errorbar=None, ax=ax, legend=False)
for container in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(container, fmt="${:,.0f}", padding=3)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Average daily sales ($)", title="Average daily sales by region")
ax.set_ylim(0, 6800)
plt.show()

The bar chart answers “which group has the biggest average?” instantly, far faster than the table. But the regions look about the same. Is that the whole story?

NoteData format for the bar chart

sns.barplot() wants long (tidy) data: one row per observation (one region on one day), with a categorical column that names the group and a numeric column holding the value. The table above is already in this shape: 4 regions × 60 days = 240 rows.

Column Type Role in the chart
region text: North, East, West, South x (and hue for color): one bar per unique value
daily_sales integer (dollars) y: averaged within each region to set the bar height
day integer, 1–60 not used by this chart

You don’t compute the averages yourself: barplot() groups the rows by region and takes the mean of daily_sales for each group (errorbar=None turns off the uncertainty lines it would otherwise add). The order= list must match the values in region exactly, spelling and capitalization included.

If your spreadsheet is wide instead, with one column per region, reshape it with melt() first (see the Lines Over Time page). If all you have is a summary table with one average per region, you can still draw the bars, but you’ve lost the individual days, and with them the spread.

Step 2: Boxplots show the spread

TipReveal the boxplots
Show the Python code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.boxplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
            hue="region", palette=palette, width=0.55, fliersize=0, ax=ax, legend=False)
sns.stripplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
              color="black", alpha=0.35, size=3.5, jitter=0.18, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Daily sales ($)",
       title="Similar averages, very different stories")
plt.show()

Now the real differences appear:

  • West is wildly inconsistent: some days are the best in the company, others the worst. Its average hides that.
  • South is actually the lowest on a normal day. Its average is propped up by 5 huge outlier days (a sale event? a data entry error?), worth investigating.
  • North and East are steady and predictable.

A bar chart of means compresses each group to one number. A boxplot shows the median, spread, and outliers, and overlaying the points shows every single day.

NoteData format for the boxplots

The boxplots use the same long table as the bar chart: one row per region per day, with region on x and daily_sales on y. Here the data must be raw, not summarized. A boxplot computes the median, quartiles, whiskers, and outliers from every individual value in each group, and the overlaid sns.stripplot() draws one dot per row. A table of averages (one number per region) can make a bar chart but can never make a boxplot.

Column Type Role in the chart
region text (categorical) x (and hue for color): one box per unique value
daily_sales integer (dollars) y: the values summarized by each box and drawn as dots
day integer, 1–60 not used by this chart

Each group needs enough rows for its box to mean something: with only a handful of values, the quartiles and “outliers” are unreliable.

NoteThe numbers, for comparison

The same story is in the numbers if you know which ones to compute. But you need to already suspect what to look for:

Show the Python code 
(sales.groupby("region")["daily_sales"]
      .agg(mean="mean", median="median", sd="std", min="min", max="max")
      .loc[region_order]
      .round(0))

title: "Bar Charts & Boxplots"
subtitle: "Comparing groups, and why the average isn't the whole story"

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sim_data import store_sales

pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 500)
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", font_scale=1.05)
region_order = ["North", "East", "West", "South"]
palette = dict(zip(region_order, sns.color_palette("Set2", 4)))
```

## Experiment: Which region is performing best?

A retail chain recorded daily sales for 60 days in each of four regions (240 rows). A manager wants to know which region is doing best and which needs attention.

::: {.raw-table}
```{python}
sales = store_sales()
sales
```
:::

::: {.guess}
**Your guess:** Which region has the highest typical daily sales? Which region is the *least predictable* from day to day? Do any regions have unusual days?
:::

## Step 1: A bar chart of averages

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reveal the bar chart

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
            hue="region", palette=palette, errorbar=None, ax=ax, legend=False)
for container in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(container, fmt="${:,.0f}", padding=3)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Average daily sales ($)", title="Average daily sales by region")
ax.set_ylim(0, 6800)
plt.show()
```

[The bar chart answers "which group has the biggest average?" instantly, far faster than the table. But the regions look *about the same*. Is that the whole story?]{.reveal-note}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Data format for the bar chart
`sns.barplot()` wants **long** (tidy) data: **one row per observation** (one region on one day), with a **categorical column** that names the group and a **numeric column** holding the value. The table above is already in this shape: 4 regions × 60 days = 240 rows.

| Column | Type | Role in the chart |
|---|---|---|
| `region` | text: North, East, West, South | `x` (and `hue` for color): one bar per unique value |
| `daily_sales` | integer (dollars) | `y`: averaged within each region to set the bar height |
| `day` | integer, 1–60 | not used by this chart |

You don't compute the averages yourself: `barplot()` groups the rows by `region` and takes the mean of `daily_sales` for each group (`errorbar=None` turns off the uncertainty lines it would otherwise add). The `order=` list must match the values in `region` exactly, spelling and capitalization included.

If your spreadsheet is **wide** instead, with one column per region, reshape it with `melt()` first (see the [Lines Over Time](time.qmd) page). If all you have is a summary table with one average per region, you can still draw the bars, but you've lost the individual days, and with them the spread.
:::

## Step 2: Boxplots show the spread

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reveal the boxplots

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.boxplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
            hue="region", palette=palette, width=0.55, fliersize=0, ax=ax, legend=False)
sns.stripplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
              color="black", alpha=0.35, size=3.5, jitter=0.18, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Daily sales ($)",
       title="Similar averages, very different stories")
plt.show()
```

[Now the real differences appear:]{.reveal-note}

- **West** is wildly inconsistent: some days are the best in the company, others the worst. Its average hides that.
- **South** is actually the *lowest* on a normal day. Its average is propped up by **5 huge outlier days** (a sale event? a data entry error?), worth investigating.
- **North** and **East** are steady and predictable.

[A bar chart of means compresses each group to **one number**. A boxplot shows the **median, spread, and outliers**, and overlaying the points shows every single day.]{.reveal-note}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Data format for the boxplots
The boxplots use the **same long table** as the bar chart: one row per region per day, with `region` on `x` and `daily_sales` on `y`. Here the data **must be raw, not summarized**. A boxplot computes the median, quartiles, whiskers, and outliers from **every individual value** in each group, and the overlaid `sns.stripplot()` draws **one dot per row**. A table of averages (one number per region) can make a bar chart but can never make a boxplot.

| Column | Type | Role in the chart |
|---|---|---|
| `region` | text (categorical) | `x` (and `hue` for color): one box per unique value |
| `daily_sales` | integer (dollars) | `y`: the values summarized by each box and drawn as dots |
| `day` | integer, 1–60 | not used by this chart |

Each group needs enough rows for its box to mean something: with only a handful of values, the quartiles and "outliers" are unreliable.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The numbers, for comparison

The same story *is* in the numbers if you know which ones to compute. But you need to already suspect what to look for:

```{python}
#| echo: true
(sales.groupby("region")["daily_sales"]
      .agg(mean="mean", median="median", sd="std", min="min", max="max")
      .loc[region_order]
      .round(0))
```
:::
 

Built with Quarto, pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn. All data are simulated.
